title: Starting my doctorate at the University of Bonn
text: In October 2026 I started my doctorate — a Doctor of Agricultural Sciences (Dr. agr.) at the University of Bonn, supervised by Prof. Dr. Frank Ewert. The research itself is carried out at the Leibniz Centre for Agricultural Landscape Research (ZALF) in Müncheberg, Germany.

title: Starting my doctorate at the University of Bonn
text:
Research focus
Landscape-scale agroecosystem modelling: spatial and temporal landscape dynamics, crop productivity and resilience.

title: Starting my doctorate at the University of Bonn
section: The question I am working on
text:
The question I am working on

How can spatial and temporal landscape information be represented and integrated into agroecosystem models to improve the understanding and prediction of crop productivity and resilience across scales?

I will share updates, code and results here as the project develops.

title: KrishnagopalHalder.
text:
Hi there, I'm
    KrishnagopalHalder.
    PhD Researcher in landscape-scale agroecosystem modelling, at ZALF & the University of Bonn.
    A geospatial data scientist building machine learning, deep learning and hybrid process-based models for crop yield forecasting, crop mapping and climate impact assessment — with open science and open-source software at heart.
    
      
      
      
      
      
      
    
  
  
    
      
      
      
    
  



  Selected Publications
  All publications





  
    2026
    
      CropFusionNet: an interpretable deep learning framework for uncertainty-aware crop yield forecasting across Germany
      
        Artificial Intelligence in Agriculture
      
      
        DOI
        
        
        Code
        
        Plain-language summary
      
      
      
        
          Overview<p>Droughts and heatwaves are becoming more frequent, and the systems used today to forecast harvests often miss how badly yields drop in those extreme years. We built CropFusionNet, a deep learning model that forecasts crop yields for every district in Germany and also shows <em>which</em> weather and environmental factors are driving each forecast.</p>
          Key findings<ul><li>It beat other deep learning models and the operational forecasting systems MARS and ABSOLUT.</li><li>Accuracy was high for silage maize (R² = 0.75, about 9% average error) and winter wheat (R² = 0.60, about 8% error), and moderate for winter barley (R² = 0.45).</li><li>It correctly showed the sharp yield losses in the drought years 2003, 2018 and 2022.</li><li>Reliable forecasts are possible 40–60 days before harvest for winter cereals and up to 70 days ahead for maize.</li></ul>
          Methods<p>The design builds on the Temporal Fusion Transformer, an AI model built for time series. It combines daily weather over the growing season with information that stays fixed, such as soil and location. It also reports how uncertain each forecast is, and explains its predictions by crediting them to the factors that drove them.</p>
          Implications<p>Earlier and more trustworthy harvest forecasts give farmers, markets and policymakers time to act before a bad season. They are especially useful in drought years, when they matter most. The code is open source.</p>
        
      
      
    
  

  
    2026
    
      AgriPINN: A process-informed neural network for interpretable and scalable crop biomass prediction under water stress
      
        Smart Agricultural Technology
      
      
        DOI
        
        
        
        
        Plain-language summary
      
      
      
        
          Overview<p>Knowing how much a crop has grown, measured as its above-ground biomass, helps farmers and water managers decide when and how much to irrigate. Pure AI models are fast but act like black boxes. Traditional crop models are easier to interpret but need a lot of detailed input data. AgriPINN combines the two: it is a neural network that has to follow a known equation for how plants grow.</p>
          Key findings<ul><li>Its prediction error was about 30% lower for winter wheat and 23% lower for maize than a strong CNN–Transformer AI baseline.</li><li>It also beat the best of the other models tested, by 9% for wheat and 2% for maize.</li><li>Along the way it estimates quantities that explain growth, such as leaf area, absorbed sunlight, how efficiently the crop uses that light, and how much water stress it is under, even though these were never used as training targets.</li></ul>
          Methods<p>A crop-growth equation from the LINTUL5 crop model is built into the network's training. The network first learns from 65 years of simulated crop data covering 397 German regions. It is then fine-tuned on three years of wheat and maize field trials grown under rain shelters, rainfed and irrigated conditions.</p>
          Implications<p>Building plant physiology into AI makes biomass predictions more accurate and easier to interpret under drought. So far the method has only been tested in Germany's temperate climate.</p>
        
      
      
    
  

  
    2025
    
      A machine learning framework for modeling and upscaling mangrove carbon productivity (ML-MCP)
      
        Agricultural and Forest Meteorology
      
      
        DOI
        
        
        
        
        Plain-language summary
      
      
      
        
          Overview<p>Mangrove forests along tropical coasts absorb large amounts of carbon, but measuring how much they take up over large areas is difficult. Earlier machine learning studies of mangrove productivity were small in scope and mostly limited to single regions. This study presents ML-MCP, a machine learning framework that models mangrove carbon uptake (gross primary productivity) and scales it up from individual sites to larger areas.</p>
          Key findings<ul><li>ML-MCP predicted mangrove carbon uptake more accurately than traditional process-based models.</li><li>Sunlight available for photosynthesis was a critical driver, and its effect on productivity was complex and non-linear.</li></ul>
          Methods<p>The framework combines the strengths of process-based and satellite-based approaches. It uses eddy-covariance measurements of carbon exchange between the forest and the atmosphere, together with environmental and satellite data. The dataset is openly available on Zenodo.</p>
          Implications<p>Better estimates of how much carbon mangroves absorb support "blue carbon" accounting and make the case for protecting and restoring these coastal forests.</p>
